text: The following is a quarterly report filed by 3M Company pursuant to Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 for the period ended June 30, 2023. The report is submitted to the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) under Commission file number 1-3285. The registrant, 3M Company, is incorporated in the state of Delaware and has an IRS Employer Identification Number of 41-0417775. Its principal executive offices are located at 3M Center, St. Paul, Minnesota 55144-1000, and its telephone number is (651) 733-1110. The company’s common stock is traded on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol MMM, as well as on the Chicago Stock Exchange, Inc., and on the SIX Swiss Exchange. The company also has outstanding debt instruments, including 1.500% Notes due 2026 (symbol MMM26), 1.750% Notes due 2030 (symbol MMM30), and 1.500% Notes due 2031 (symbol MMM31), all listed on the New York Stock Exchange. As of June 30, 2023, the outstanding shares of common stock were 551,992,430. The report indicates that the company has filed all required reports under Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act during the preceding 12 months and has been subject to such filing requirements for the past 90 days. It has also submitted electronically all required Interactive Data Files under Rule 405 of Regulation S-T. 3M Company is classified as a large accelerated filer and is not considered a smaller reporting company or an emerging growth company. The company is not a shell company. In the first quarter of 2023, 3M announced structural reorganization actions to reduce the corporate center size, simplify the supply chain, streamline its geographic footprint, reduce management layers, align go-to-market models with customers, and reduce manufacturing roles to match production volumes. During the first six months of 2023, management approved actions affecting approximately 5,100 positions, resulting in pre-tax charges of $52 million in the first quarter and $212 million in the second quarter. Remaining activities are expected to be largely completed by the end of 2023, with the full initiative from the first quarter of 2023 through 2025 expected to impact approximately 8,500 positions worldwide and incur a pre-tax charge of $700 million to $900 million. The restructuring charges were recorded in the income statement as $47 million and $63 million in cost of sales, $146 million and $178 million in selling, general and administrative expenses, $19 million and $23 million in research, development and related expenses, totaling $212 million and $264 million in operating income impact. The Company is involved in numerous legal claims and lawsuits, primarily in the United States and worldwide, involving products liability, intellectual property, commercial, antitrust, federal healthcare regulations, securities, and environmental matters. The Company vigorously defends all such proceedings and responds cooperatively to subpoenas and requests for information, which may lead to additional claims or proceedings and result in significant costs. Outcomes are often uncertain, and noncompliance with laws or regulations could result in fines, penalties, or injunctive relief. In assessing liabilities related to legal proceedings, the Company follows ASC 450, Contingencies, and records a liability when a loss is both probable and reasonably estimable. If a range of loss is identified, the Company records the most likely estimate or the low end of the range if no single best estimate exists. The Company either discloses the amount of a possible loss or a range of loss.

The Company is involved in numerous and diverse legal proceedings with various plaintiffs, each asserting specific claims and legal theories based on unique allegations that may not apply to other cases, and may seek substantial compensatory and, in some instances, punitive damages. These factors, along with the interdependence of outcomes across related matters—such as timing, amount of liability, or both—contribute to the complexity of the lawsuits, making it difficult for the Company to predict outcomes or reasonably estimate potential losses. In accordance with ASC 450, Contingencies, and related guidance, the Company records liabilities only when a loss is both probable and can be reasonably estimated. If a range of loss is identified, the Company records the most likely estimate or the low end of the range if no single best estimate exists. The Company discloses possible losses or ranges exceeding accruals when estimable, or states that an estimate cannot be made. Significant legal proceedings are disclosed even when liability is not probable or the amount is not estimable, if there is at least a reasonable possibility of a loss. The Company regularly reviews its estimates of probable liabilities and associated expenses and receivables each period, adjusting accruals when a previously unestimable or non-probable loss becomes estimable or probable. As a result, current accruals and estimates of loss, as well as their potential impact on the Company’s consolidated financial position, results of operations, and cash flows, are likely to change over time. Due to inherent uncertainties, the Company may ultimately incur charges significantly exceeding currently recorded liabilities, including for matters without existing accruals because losses are not currently probable or reasonably estimable. Many claims are at various stages, seek indeterminate or excessive damages, and may take years to resolve. Information from plaintiff demands, discovery, expert reports, or settlement discussions may lead the Company to assess whether a reasonable estimate of a probable loss or range exists, though such information may not result in a determination. Even when a loss is not probable or reasonably estimable, developments or resolutions in a matter could be material to the Company and adversely affect its financial position, results of operations, and cash flows. Future adverse rulings or settlements in one or more matters could also lead to changes in the assessment of probable and reasonably estimable losses in other matters. For insurance receivables related to legal proceedings, the Company estimates based on policy terms, exclusions, case law, experience with similar claims, and the nature of the claim and remaining coverage, recording amounts expected to be received under ASC 450, ASC 610-30, and related guidance. For insured matters with accrued liabilities, the Company records receivables for the amount of insurance it expects to receive. For matters without accrued liabilities but involving defense expenses, the Company records receivables for the insurance covering those expenses. As of June 30, 2023, the Company is a named defendant in numerous lawsuits involving approximately 4,066 individual claimants, compared to about 4,028 claimants with actions pending as of December 31, 2022. Most claims allege exposure to asbestos, silica, coal mine dust, or other occupational dusts from products manufactured by other defendants or in the workplace, while a minority allege personal injury from asbestos exposure to products previously manufactured by the Company, often unspecified. The Company’s volume of new and pending claims is substantially lower than at its peak in 2003, and future filings are expected to remain at much lower levels. Consequently, claims involving serious injuries—such as mesothelioma, other malignancies, and black lung disease—will represent a larger percentage of total claims than in the past. Over twenty years, the Company has won fifteen of sixteen jury trials, including two in 2018: one in California in February and one in Massachusetts in December, both involving allegations that 3M respirators failed to protect against asbestos fibers. In April 2018, a Kentucky jury found 3M’s 8710 respirators failed to protect two coal miners from coal mine dust, awarding $2 million in compensatory and $63 million in punitive damages. The trial court entered judgment, and the Company appealed. In 2019, the Company settled a substantial majority of pending Kentucky and West Virginia coal mine dust lawsuits for $340 million, including the April 2018 verdict and the appeal was dismissed. In 2003, the State of West Virginia, through its Attorney General, filed a complaint in the Circuit Court of Lincoln County against the Company and two other manufacturers of respiratory protection products, which was amended in 2005. The amended complaint seeks substantial, unspecified compensatory damages primarily for reimbursement of state costs related to worker’s compensation and healthcare for workers with occupational pneumoconiosis, plus unspecified punitive damages. In October 2019, the court granted the State’s motion to sever its unfair trade practices claim, which seeks civil penalties of up to $5,000 per violation under the state’s Consumer Credit Protection Act, based on allegations that statements about 3M’s respirators were misleading. The State’s expert has estimated that 3M sold over five million respirators in the state during the relevant period, asserting each sale constitutes a separate violation; 3M disputes both the expert’s estimate and the State’s interpretation of a separate violation. 3M has raised various defenses, including that its marketing did not violate the Act and that the claims are barred by the statute of limitations. No liability has been recorded because the Company believes liability is not probable and reasonably estimable, and it cannot estimate a possible loss or range of loss due to lack of meaningful discovery responses from the State, uncertainties regarding joint and several liability among defendants, and the potential allocation of fault by a factfinder. 3M has adopted a new strategy to manage its liabilities related to the Combat Arms Version 2 earplugs and Aearo respirator mask/asbestos matters by committing to satisfy all claims determined to be entitled to compensation. During the voluntary chapter 11 proceedings, 3M had an accrual for commitments related to funding a trust that included Aearo respirator mask/asbestos matters. As of June 30, 2023, following the dismissal, the Company, through its Aearo subsidiary, had accruals of $44 million for product liabilities and defense costs related to current and future Aearo-related asbestos, silica-related, and coal mine dust claims. Responsibility for legal costs, settlements, and judgments is shared among Aearo, Cabot, American Optical Corporation, and a subsidiary of Warner Lambert and their respective insurers, known as the “Payor Group,” based on the number of years each company sold respiratory products under the “AO Safety” brand or owned the AO Safety Division and the alleged years of exposure of individual plaintiffs. Aearo’s contingent liability is further limited by an agreement dated July 11, 1995, with Cabot, which provides that as long as Aearo pays Cabot a quarterly fee of $100,000, Cabot will retain responsibility and indemnify Aearo for product liability claims involving exposure to asbestos, silica, or silica products for respirators sold prior to July 11, 1995. Aearo and Cabot have applied this agreement to claims arising from the use of respirators involving exposure to asbestos, silica, or silica products prior to January 1, 1997. As a result, Aearo’s potential liability is limited to exposures alleged to have arisen from the use of respirators involving exposure to asbestos, silica, or silica products on or after January 1, 1997. To date, Aearo has elected to pay the quarterly fee; however, it could still be exposed to additional claims for part of the pre-July 11, 1995 period if it discontinues participation in the arrangement or if Cabot is unable to meet its obligations. Developments that could affect the estimate of Aearo’s liabilities include significant changes in the number of future claims, average cost of resolving claims, legal defense costs, mix and nature of claims, trial and appellate outcomes, changes in applicable law and procedure, changes in liability allocation among co-defendants, financial viability of Payor Group members including exhaustion of insurance coverage, or an inaccurate interpretation of the contractual obligations. The Company cannot determine the impact of these developments on its current estimate of Aearo’s liability, and if any occurred, the actual liabilities could be significantly larger than the accrued amount. Due to the difficulty in projecting unasserted claims, the complexity of allocating future claims among the Payor Group, and the potential for these developments, the Company cannot estimate the amount or range by which Aearo’s liability may exceed the established accrual.
